idiom_name: typed recursive split/combine skeleton + a typed worker-pool boundary (worker_threads / Web Workers)
implementation_notes: Same runtime as JavaScript, so the fork/join is hand-written around worker_threads or Web Workers; TypeScript's contribution is at the contract: split and combine become generic signatures (split: (T) => [T, T] | null, combine: (R, R) => R) that make the recursion's shape checkable, and the worker boundary must be typed with structured-cloneable payloads - no functions, no class instances carrying prototype state. There is no standard-library task pool, so a Worker pool (or a pool library) replaces the classic pool and every crossing pays the clone cost.
pitfalls: Types vanish at the worker boundary: a typed message still fails structured clone if it carries a function, a class instance or a symbol-keyed property.
Turning the recursion into a Promise-returning one changes the whole call chain (and cannot be awaited from non-async callbacks) - decide the async boundary before parallelising.
tsconfig target/lib do not provide a thread API: the pool must be typed against Node's worker_threads or the DOM lib explicitly, or the code stops compiling on the browser build.
